title: The Sunday Essay: In Defence of Jung
author: Leadership, Rewritten
summary: Claydon defends Jung against dismissal as either a mystic or the grandfather of personality typing, arguing that his real subject is adaptation: how people become socially legible through personas and what gets pushed into shadow along the way. Using the story of Arun, an admired leader who grows brittle and moralising as his role becomes overloaded, he shows how a rewarded mask can crowd out the rest of the self. He then reads Jungian recurring situations, namely mask over-identification, projection, rivalry and scapegoating, and breakdown and renewal, through Giddens, Beck, Bauman and Rosa to explain why late-modern organisations intensify them. The practical advice is to avoid starting with type and instead ask what mask a system rewards and what it makes hard to admit. This is an interpretive piece, but it gives leaders a concrete way to read difficult behaviour as situational rather than as character failure.
points: Jung's value for organisations lies in reading masks, shadows and recurring dramas rather than in typology.
When competence becomes something a leader must constantly prove, professionalism turns into a defence against uncertainty and need, and brittleness follows.
Shadow returns indirectly through overreaction, projection and moralisation, which is why rivalry and scapegoating persist in unstable systems.
Burnout can be read as the collapse of a one-sided adaptation, which calls for a less partial relation to oneself and sometimes a redesigned role.
Maya's intervention succeeded by clarifying the overloaded role and making room for what the old professionalism had pushed underground.
quotes: They become trapped in recurring human situations — over-identification, rivalry, scapegoating, disillusionment, collapse, renewal — that are deeper than style or personality alone can explain. Read that way, Jung becomes less a typologist of selves and more a diagnostician of masks, shadows, and recurring organisational dramas.

The deeper problem was that the mask had become too important to him, and perhaps too rewarded by the system around him, for him to risk relaxing it. Competence, composure, and strategic seriousness had stopped being things he could do. They were becoming things he had to be.

The persona is the social face: the aspect of the self that learns how to function in the world and meet its demands. It is the part that knows how to sound appropriate, competent, serious, warm, firm, strategic, calm, or whatever else a situation rewards.

Late modern organisations often confuse development with the strengthening of persona: more confidence, better communication, stronger presence, cleaner self-narration, greater strategic fluency, more compelling authenticity. Some of that is clearly useful.

The mask begins to colonise the self. Over time, some of the most impressive organisational identities become the most brittle. The stronger the persona, the harder it becomes to risk any experience that does not fit it.

Burnout is often described in energetic or managerial terms: depleted capacity, chronic overload, insufficient recovery, and poor boundaries. All of that may be true. But Jung lets us ask a second question: what kind of self was this person having to be, for how long, and at what psychic cost?

They describe behavioural surfaces while missing the social and developmental pressures shaping them. A leader is described as controlling, visionary, emotionally reserved, highly relational, introverted, overbearing, and conflict-averse. Perhaps all of that contains some truth.
